name: agent-orchestrator
description: Repository-agnostic orchestrator foundation for a writing Claude Code agent and a read-only Codex reviewer.
//exports: Only the CLI entry point and the generated contract are public. Deep imports of dist/core/** — in particular the internal structural task-state schema — are deliberately not offered as API (AO-009).

scripts.//build: Two artefacts, and the native one is not optional. `build:boundary` compiles the Windows launch boundary (native/ao-launch/AoLaunch.cs) with the in-box .NET Framework compiler into dist/native/ao-launch.exe, and fails the build if that compiler is absent. A dist that silently lacked the boundary would let a later slice ship a runner whose ownership guarantee resolves to nothing.
scripts.verify:dist-doctor: npm run build && npm run test:dist-doctor
scripts.verify:dist-trusted-profile: npm run build && npm run test:dist-trusted-profile
scripts.//test:dist-lease-race: The execution lease under real concurrency: 16 OS processes race for one lease, 8 times. A second acquire inside one process proves the exclusive create refuses an existing file; it cannot prove the claim is atomic, because two synchronous calls in one thread cannot interleave. This is the check that would have caught V2-07's advisory compare-and-swap, applied to its replacement.
scripts.verify:dist-lease-race: npm run build && npm run test:dist-lease-race
scripts.//test:dist-lease-release: The other half of the lease's life, against the shipped artefact: 6 OS processes contend, the owner gives the lease back, and the directory is read. It exists because giving a lease back is an effect on a shared directory, and no return value can show it happened — dropping the `discard` that deletes the detached record survived the entire pre-existing suite and fails this in every round, with the leftovers accumulating. (This comment first claimed that `removeVerifiedLease` reduced to `return 'REMOVED'` 'passes every in-process assertion', which was written before it was measured and is wrong: an existing test catches that one. It still fails this gate four ways per round.) The real-process measurement of the release effect was previously incidental to the break harness, and was lost when that harness was withdrawn with the break.
scripts.verify:dist-lease-release: npm run build && npm run test:dist-lease-release
scripts.//test:dist-lease-containment: V3 slice 4 end to end, against the shipped artefact and a real contained process. It exists because the in-process suite drives the substituted `start` seam - the boundary executable resolves relative to the compiled adapter and is absent under src - and that seam supplies the very values the mint reads, so those cases prove the gate and not that a real launch attests anything. Deleting the mint call from runOwnedCommand leaves the whole vitest suite green on the questions it may ask; this fails. Five cases: a real owned node run carries an attestation coupled to this process; the record is published beside the lease, reads back CONTAINED from bytes on disk, and the LEASE DOCUMENT IS BYTE-IDENTICAL afterwards - the pin that the withdrawn in-lease rewrite, whose interrupted form leaves an unreleasable lease nothing in this build can clear, does not come back; a one-field edit reads NOT_THIS_LEASE and a torn record reads MALFORMED while the lease stays HELD; a successor lease at the same path is refused, its bytes are unchanged and no record is published against it; and a command that never ran carries nothing. Windows only, and it says so rather than pretending to measure containment elsewhere.
scripts.verify:dist-lease-containment: npm run build && npm run test:dist-lease-containment
scripts.//test:dist-stale-recovery: V3 slice 5 against the shipped artefact, with a REAL dead owner. It exists because the in-process suite never lets a second operating-system process HOLD the lease: it starts one - that is where its genuinely dead pid comes from - but that child never touches the lease, and the owner named in every stale fixture is the vitest worker with the pid overwritten afterwards, so the chain from a real acquisition, through the death of the process that made it, to a real removal is never travelled end to end by one owner; and it runs against src rather than against what is shipped. (Two earlier justifications here were false and each was caught by a later review: that every dead owner there was a substituted probe and that a NOT_FOUND stub would pass the whole vitest suite - true when written, falsified by the fix that made those fixtures use the real probe - and then that the suite never runs a second process at all, which its own next clause contradicted.) Four phases per round: a separate OS process acquires the lease and exits still holding it, having either proved two writer launches (recovered, no leftovers, and a fresh acquisition then succeeds), opened one and abandoned it (refused as LAUNCH_HISTORY_UNPROVEN, lease byte-identical), or deleted its history to stand in for an older build (refused as LAUNCH_HISTORY_ABSENT). The load-bearing case is the fourth: the owner is kept ALIVE and the recovery must refuse with OWNER_RUNNING. Without it every RECOVERED above could be an instrument that cannot tell a living process from a dead one. Disabling the liveness gate in the built artefact fails this check four ways per run, which was measured rather than assumed.
scripts.verify:dist-stale-recovery: npm run build && npm run test:dist-stale-recovery
scripts.//test:dist-crash-recovery: M2 slice 1 against the shipped artefact, with a REAL owner killed while a REAL contained writer is running. It exists because everything it measures is about processes that outlive - or fail to outlive - the process making the assertion, and the in-process suite cannot reach any of it: there the establishment mark is written by a vitest worker against pids it chose, and the 'writer' is a value. Here an owner really takes the lease, a target is really placed in a Job Object by the kernel, and the owner is really terminated with taskkill /F and no /T, so what happens to the tree is measured rather than arranged. The recovery runs through the SHIPPED CLI with no attendance flag and nothing on stdin, because that is the U1 claim: a scheduler meeting a crashed repository can get it running again. Four phases per round. Phase B is the control that matters: the ledger names processes that are deliberately still alive (started detached, so the owner's death does not take them), the recovery must refuse LAUNCH_TREE_STILL_RUNNING and leave the lease byte-identical, and the SAME lease must then become recoverable once those processes are killed - so the refusal is attributable to liveness and not to anything else about the fixture. Without it every RECOVERED in phase A could be an instrument that cannot tell a live process from a dead one. Phase C requires a living owner to refuse OWNER_RUNNING with launchHistory still null, which pins that the new arm is unreachable past a live owner. Phase D pins the window this slice does NOT close. It stands in for it rather than reproducing it: the owner announces a generation and starts no process at all, which is the state an owner killed between the announcement and the kernel's answer would leave, and is the only way to reach that state deterministically - racing a real kill into a 76ms window would be a flaky gate measuring the scheduler. It must stay LAUNCH_HISTORY_UNPROVEN, which is why U1 is narrowed rather than closed. Phase E is separate from the rounds and measures the one thing the four phases cannot: that the establishment mint and the ending mint describe the SAME launch. The upgrade ESTABLISHED -> CONTAINED is refused unless the confirming attestation carries the digest already standing on the entry, the two are minted at different moments from different reads (owned.launchNonce against the nonce echoed in the status file), and if they ever disagreed every real launch would stop at ESTABLISHED and never reach CONTAINED - silently, because the confirmation's result is discarded by design. Phases A-D would all still pass, because none of them confirms anything. E drives begin -> establish -> confirm through a real owned command and requires the ledger to end at CONTAINED. Windows only, and it says so rather than pretending to measure containment elsewhere.
scripts.verify:dist-crash-recovery: npm run build && npm run test:dist-crash-recovery
scripts.//test:dist-lifecycle-restart: V3 slice 6 against the shipped artefact, with a real owner process that dies still holding the lease. It exists because the in-process suite fabricates a stale lease by rewriting one field of a document the vitest worker itself wrote - the right instrument for the refusals, which never get past the ledger, and the wrong one for the permission, whose owner is then this process with the pid overwritten. Here one owner takes the lease through the real exclusive create, proves a launch, and dies; the lifecycle driver recovers it, acquires again through the ordinary path, and gives it back. The proof that the acquisition really happened is that `startTask` was reached at all: it is unreachable without a lease, so a run that treated the removal as a grant cannot produce a start result. The task named is absent from the plan, so the run stops there and no agent is ever started. Four phases per round. Phase C is the control that matters here: the owner is kept ALIVE with the same proved launch history phase A was permitted on, so the only difference is that it is running, and the driver must refuse it without reaching the recovery at all - asserted as recovery === null. It is NOT the control for the recovery predicate's own liveness discrimination; that is test:dist-stale-recovery phase D, and an earlier version of this sentence claimed it here. Phase B refuses an unproven launch history and Phase D withholds the grant, both requiring the lease to come out byte-identical.
scripts.verify:dist-lifecycle-restart: npm run build && npm run test:dist-lifecycle-restart
scripts.//test:dist-unattended-auto-resume: V3 slice 8's authority boundary against the shipped CLI, in real processes. It exists because the slice's headline behaviour - sleep, then resume - cannot be measured in a real process at all: every path that reaches a resume runs the real auth preflight, which starts the subscription CLIs, so a harness driving it would spend quota on a developer machine and stop at AUTH_PREFLIGHT_FAILED on CI. That is a gate measuring the machine rather than the build, and the honest answer is to say so and measure what IS deterministic everywhere because it is decided before any preflight. Two parts. Six argument refusals - two grants at once, a wait without the grant, a wait without a bound, a bound without a wait, and stale recovery combined with either - are driven against a repository path that does not exist, so the absence of the resolver's own failure text in the output measures the ordering directly rather than assuming it. Then the load-bearing negative: --automatic-resume-only on a task the product itself reports as startable must create no state, no branch and no worktree. Its positive control is inside the same invocation - the report must carry `Release      : RELEASED`, which only a run that really acquired the execution lease can print, so the untouched repository is attributable to the start refusal rather than to an earlier fall-over. The wake-and-resume cycle stays in tests/v3-08-unattended-auto-resume.test.ts with an injected clock and sleep and a real lease.
scripts.verify:dist-unattended-auto-resume: npm run build && npm run test:dist-unattended-auto-resume
scripts.//test:dist-runtime-gate: The V2 runtime gate against the shipped CLI. It exists because the gate terminates the process and writes synchronously to fd 2 at the CLI entry, and none of that is observable from inside a vitest worker. A self-verifying preload substitutes process.platform/process.version and dies with exit 97 if the substitution did not take, so an ineffective preload cannot manufacture a green result. The negative cases assert that the lease report is ABSENT from stdout - that the action did not run - rather than only that a message was printed.
scripts.verify:dist-runtime-gate: npm run build && npm run test:dist-runtime-gate
scripts.//test:dist-notify-egress: The first network egress this product has, measured against the shipped CLI in a real process. A self-verifying preload points the OS profile at a scratch directory (dying with exit 97 if the substitution did not take, checked through the ESM binding the product actually uses) and arms every socket surface - fetch, net, http, https, dns. Without a notify.yaml the run must complete having opened nothing: removing the opt-in check makes this case die with exit 96 rather than pass, which is the measurement it exists for. With one, exactly one POST reaches a loopback server and its bytes are read. It deliberately does NOT claim to kill the detail form-gate mutant - neither ending reachable here carries free text, so that mutant is killed in tests/v2-10-operator-notification.test.ts instead.
scripts.verify:dist-notify-egress: npm run build && npm run test:dist-notify-egress
scripts.//test:dist-boundary: The V3 launch boundary against the shipped artefact, with real processes and real deaths. It exists because every property it measures is about processes that outlive — or fail to outlive — the process making the assertion: the helper is killed in one case and the AO stand-in in another, and the question is what is still running afterwards. Survivors are counted by heartbeat rather than by pid, because the spike found that a terminated process whose object is still referenced looks alive in a process walk. The load-bearing case is the negative control: it builds a deliberately weakened helper (inheritable job handle AND no handle list, the pair the spike measured as the one that breaks containment) into a temporary directory, kills it, and REQUIRES survivors — 7 of them. Without that case, every '0 survivors' here could be an instrument that cannot see anything. Deliberately not measured: byte budgets, stdin vocabulary, timeouts; those stay in AO and belong to the adapter slices.
scripts.verify:dist-boundary: npm run build && npm run test:dist-boundary
scripts.//test:dist-owned-command: The V3 owned-command adapter against the shipped artefact, with real processes. It exists because the adapter resolves the boundary executable from its own location: run from `src` there is none, so every case would refuse with BOUNDARY_EXECUTABLE_MISSING and pass while measuring nothing. Nine of the twenty cases send the same invocation down both paths — `runCommand`, the contract AO has today, and `runOwnedCommand`, the one this slice adds — and require them to agree about output, budgets, exit codes, timeouts and stdin delivery. Most share one argument vector between the two halves, so a survivor is identified by its own heartbeat file rather than by which runner left it. That differential is not an attempt to reproduce `taskkill` containment, which the ADR replaces; it is the guard against the adapter inventing a different command semantics on the way, which the adapter's own green tests cannot see. Two findings came from it rather than from review: node reports a Windows exit code unsigned while the helper writes it as a signed int32 (0xC0000005 differed by path), and a stdin write destroyed by this side's OWN termination was being reported as a proven channel failure. No target process is started by any case without a heartbeat directory, on either path of a differential, and every such directory is swept at the end of the run; the cases that start one tree also get a per-case window. Six earlier versions of this sentence overstated that coverage, each time one class further down. It deliberately does NOT claim the containment settings are load-bearing — that needs the negative control in `test:dist-boundary`, and stays there.
scripts.verify:dist-owned-command: npm run build && npm run test:dist-owned-command
scripts.//test:writer-authority: The real Claude CLI authority split, measured through the production adapter. NOT part of `verify`: each invocation starts a real agent, takes 4-33s and spends subscription quota. It exists because every other control substitutes the agent seam and therefore cannot see the argv the real CLI receives. Two stages: the writer edits inside the worktree and CANNOT commit (no shell, no MCP, escape blocked, tree left dirty), then the AO production path measures the delta, enforces scope, commits, and leaves HEAD moved and the tree clean. A third, standing control drives the pre-fix vector literally and must keep reproducing the dogfood root cause. Run before any dogfood is called clean.
scripts.verify:writer-authority: npm run build && npm run test:writer-authority
scripts.//test:foundation-safe: Excludes exactly two files, and each for a MEASURED reason rather than a suspicion. tests/windows-tree-kill-tool-release.test.ts is not unstable itself - it drives real-process churn of its own (a child Node harness process per case plus a detached, deliberately surviving Node helper standing in for the tool process; the supervisor's tool seam is injected, so no real taskkill.exe is started for that mechanism), which intermittently destabilised unrelated files running in parallel with it (AO-008-S2-R1-F1). tests/v4-09-post-merge-verification.test.ts is the second, added by V4 slice 9, and the measurement is on the record: it builds 27 real Git repositories and drives real `git worktree add`/`remove` through the production seam, and CI timed it at 107s against 41s here. On the run that added it, `tests/v2-09-dependent-commit-chain.test.ts` - a 190-second file this slice never touched, and one that passed on main minutes earlier - had a 10-second hook time out, skipped three cases and failed the gate. A solo run flatters a new slice; the parallel gate is where a test budget is measured. Neither exclusion weakens what is checked: both files run below, in their own serial gates, in full. tests/exec.test.ts is no longer excluded: the AO-008 exclusion was retired in AO-008-S3 after the candidate set passed 10/10 sequential runs with it collected.
scripts.//test:windows-tree-kill-tool-release: The real-process tool-release probe, in full and unweakened, with no sibling test file running beside it: --no-file-parallelism keeps its process churn from reaching any other suite.
scripts.verify: npm run schema:generate && npm run typecheck && npm run build && npm run test:dist-doctor && npm run test:dist-trusted-profile && npm run test:dist-lease-race && npm run test:dist-lease-release && npm run test:dist-lease-containment && npm run test:dist-stale-recovery && npm run test:dist-crash-recovery && npm run test:dist-lifecycle-restart && npm run test:dist-unattended-auto-resume && npm run test:dist-runtime-gate && npm run test:dist-notify-egress && npm run test:dist-boundary && npm run test:dist-owned-command && npm run test:foundation-safe && npm run test:v4-09-post-merge-verification && npm run test:windows-tree-kill-tool-release
scripts.//test:v4-09-post-merge-verification: V4 slice 9's real-Git suite, with no sibling test file running beside it. It is here rather than in the parallel gate because of what it starts, not because it is flaky: 27 real repositories, real detached worktrees created and removed through the production Git seam, and real execution leases taken and released. Every one of those is the point - an injected runner would prove how this build CLASSIFIES Git's answers and never that Git was asked anything - so the cost is not removable, only isolatable. `--no-file-parallelism` keeps its process churn from reaching any other suite, which is the exact remedy the sibling gate below already records.
